<reason>Side A built a coherent but fairly conventional case (silent metabolic disease, personal feedback beats generic advice, anxiety is a minority cost like scales/step counters), and it held up reasonably well through Rebuttal 1. But Side B's case sharpened with each round: it isolated the specific disanalogy between glucose and other biometrics (no validated "good/bad" direction for healthy people), tied that to a plausible harm mechanism (calorie-counter/eating-disorder analogy), added a concrete crowding-out story (attention/capital flowing to monetizable glucose coaching instead of structural fixes), and then landed the decisive blow in Rebuttal 2: the bread-vs-lentil "arrow" PRO relied on as the CGM's unique contribution was already public knowledge via glycemic index tables for decades, so the device's marginal information is thin while its marginal anxiety is the actual novel, scaled product. PRO's answer to the parallel pressure question (evidence that benefit outweighs anxiety) was a symmetry dodge ("we lack such trials for scales either") rather than an affirmative case, and its closing—explicitly clipped for exceeding the word limit—never fully recovered the "arrow already existed" point, gesturing at personalization-vs-behavior-change without fully developing it. B's closing, by contrast, cleanly crystallized the asymmetry it had built. B answered pressure more directly (offering a concrete alternative signal, the A1c test) and kept its throughline tighter across rounds, making the debate easier to decide in its favor.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 point (B4.1) that glycemic-index tables already publicly supplied the "bread beats lentils" arrow PRO's whole mechanism depended on—reframing the CGM as manufacturing alarm-theater around already-known facts rather than new actionable knowledge—was the most decisive exchange, and PRO's clipped closing never fully neutralized it.</best_rebuttal>
